rows.q: Katz says there is no economy. A sceptical economist replies that markets obviously coordinate millions of decisions with no center at all. How would Katz answer, and where is his answer weakest?
rows.a:
## How Katz would answer

Start with what the slogan means. "There is no 'economy.' There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)). Katz is not denying that people buy, sell and adjust to prices. He is denying that the market is a self-standing domain with its own origin, as opposed to something that happens *inside* an order set up and held in place by a center: whoever distributes, enforces and judges. His reply to the economist comes in four steps.

**1. The market is a delegated space.** Katz defines it so: "Markets are real insofar as they are what people without direct authority for maintaining the social center do with knowledge, information and skills when they are being protected and bounded but not directly supervised by such authorities" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-3)). The decisions the economist points to really are uncoordinated by anyone. But they happen in what Katz calls the "capillaries", the margins any supervision leaves open. Their being *decentralized* doesn't make them *centerless*. Property, contract and courts all have to be in place first, and these are distributions from the center that the market presupposes without producing.

**2. Markets and money are made.** Historically, "Markets are created by states so as to provision their militaries when abroad, and money is supplied so as to enable soldiers to participate in those markets" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-2)). In the long essay with Zack Baker, Katz follows Christine Desan's history of English money and Colin Drumm's theory of liquidity. Money is a record of debt to the center, and modern money comes from the state borrowing from a central bank. On Drumm's account a market exists only where a dealer quotes a spread, and the dealer can do that only on the bet that someone with deeper reserves will cover him. Katz concludes that "something like a 'lender of last resort' is constitutive of any market" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-62)). So the economist's "no center at all" holds in normal times. It stops holding at the moments when the market itself is at stake, when the bailout comes and the center turns out to have been there all along.

**3. The Hayekian point is true but beside the point.** Katz grants it: "This is of course true, but also a non-sequitur and a distraction." A general cannot know what every platoon will face either, so "there will therefore be 'markets' all along the line" inside any chain of command. The argument for markets, he says, "is really saying no more than that you can't do a very good job if you're being micromanaged at every point along the way. It's equally true that you can't do a very good job if the terms of each move you make have to be 'negotiated' with a constantly changing range of agents" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-23)). The question that matters is how much leeway the center grants at each level, not whether there is a center.

**4. Prices are measures of power.** Following Bichler and Nitzan's *Capital as Power*, Katz reads value as expected future earnings. Those expectations depend on who controls the legal and political conditions that make the earnings likely. Price "signals" are therefore readings of where command sits, not neutral information. The economist's picture of a field of equal agents is a variant of what Katz calls the Big Scene: a scene imagined so that no center ever emerges.

## Where the answer is weakest

**The slide between "conditions" and "operation."** Steps 1 to 3 show that markets *depend* on a center. A good institutional economist could grant all of that and still say that, inside the frame, prices do the coordinating and nobody plans it. "There is no economy" needs the stronger claim that coordination itself flows from the center, and Katz concedes ground here. "There will be all kinds of 'interfaces' where the market rules in the sense a liberal economist means. It may be that majority, even the vast majority, of transactions take place at such interfaces." What remains is whether "disciplinary production," even if numerically inferior, "sets the tone" ([What are We Talking About When We Talk About the Market?](/post/what-are-we-talking-about-when-we-talk-about-the-market-gablog#p-16)). That is a much more modest thesis than the slogan.

**The replacement for prices.** Katz names the economist's strongest card himself: "the notorious pricing problem, which is taken to be the doom of non-capitalistic systems" ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-16)). His answers are, first, that "the free market, represented in the fluctuation of prices, already only exists at the margins" ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-18)), and second, that public rankings of designated successors, revised constantly, "replicate price change by providing information about who will be directing a particular link in the supply chain." This "would also solve Hayek's information problem" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). That last claim is asserted, not shown. A succession ranking tells you whom to trust. It doesn't tell you how much steel, at what relative scarcity, to send where. Katz is candid about the gamble: "if that's utopian, so be it" ([Can Networks Crowd Out Markets?](/post/can-networks-crowd-out-markets-gablog#p-5)). (The socialist calculation debate, Mises and Hayek against Lange, is outside the archive. An economist will bring it up at once, and it is exactly the point Katz's mechanism has to meet.)

**The center begins to resemble the market.** To avoid central planning, Katz says "the center need not be thought of as a planning center; rather, it is the result of continual sifting, filtering, testing, mapping, simulating performed on data" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)). A center that *results from* distributed sifting is close to the economist's spontaneous order with a new name. The disagreement may come down to whether that order has a responsible, nameable occupant. That is a real disagreement, but about governance more than about coordination.

**An earlier Katz against the later one.** In 2011 he warned that proposing one economy as the model for all others is reductive and "ultimately prove[s] violent," and insisted that "There are many economies and they supplement and supplant each other in many ways" ([Economism](/post/economism#p-3)). "There is only ritual distribution from the center" looks like exactly that move, made in the other direction.

## What to read next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf): the fullest version of the argument, with the Desan and Drumm material on money, spread and succession.
- [Monopoly](/post/monopoly): Katz facing the pricing problem directly, with his "controlled usurpation" as the substitute signal. This is where to test the weak point.

A question to take further: take one market you know well, say housing in your city. List what the price could not do without someone first having distributed, enforced or guaranteed it. Then ask which of the remaining coordination Katz's succession rankings could plausibly carry.

rows.q: I run a 40-person company and two senior people are fighting over who leads a new product. Use imperative exchange, the pointman and succession to tell me what to do on Monday.
rows.a:
You are the pointman in this situation, and that is the root of what you should do on Monday. Katz's vocabulary explains why the fight is happening, why the usual fixes (co-leads, a vote, letting them settle it) make it worse, and what kind of decision ends it.

## Read the fight as an imperative exchange that has broken down

An imperative exchange is the basic relation between those at the margin and the center: you obey what the center asks, and you ask the center for something in return. In its most mature form the request becomes "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)). Both of your senior people have spent years fulfilling your imperatives: build this, ship that, carry the company. Each has now issued a reciprocal imperative back to you: *give me this product*. Katz's definition of resentment describes their condition exactly:

> "Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse." ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19))

They appear to be fighting each other, but both are really petitioning you. Katz's claim is that "All resentment is toward the center, and yet it seems like we're really resenting the guy next to us" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-15)). The quarrel between them comes from a command you have not yet issued. In his account of how demands work, he argues that a demand is really a request for a command:

> "whatever your demand of the center, consider the kind of command that could limit and satisfy it better than it would itself know how to and then realize that your demand is really for such a command." ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-17))

So the fight is a demand that you act.

## You are the pointman, so don't hand the center away

Katz takes "pointman" as his name for whoever occupies the center: "He is at the point, taking the initiative, gathering all initiatives under his banner, and at the same time the one everyone points to, out of wonder, curiosity or outrage, with the finger of accusation" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)). Taking the point means accepting that someone will point at you as well.

That rules out the three tempting exits.

**Co-leads.** "Only one person can occupy the center at a time, just like only one person can speak at a time in a conversation" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-7)). Two leads leave you with a center that stays contested, and the contest carries on into every decision about the product.

**Letting the team decide, or letting them fight it out.** Katz's thought experiment about a group rebuilding after a fire applies here. If the group elects its leader, "the task of the new leader is not to build the building, but to maintain a majority among those he is serving" ([same text, p-12](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-12)). Whoever wins that way spends the product's life managing a constituency.

**Waiting.** Katz defines power as adjudication: "you have power insofar as, and to the degree that, contending parties bring their grievances, counter-grievances and defenses to you rather than resort or revert to the vendetta" ([A New Model of Power](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-3)). They have brought the dispute to you. If you don't judge it, they will settle it by vendetta, through sniping, slow-walking and recruiting allies.

## Why this is a succession problem as much as a product problem

Katz applies succession beyond states: "since all institutions are governing institutions, [singularized succession in perpetuity] is the privileged mode of maintaining social continuity" ([The Thing That It Is](/post/the-thing-that-it-is-toward-a-curriculum-for-the-officer-class#p-5)). He also offers a diagnosis you should consider seriously:

> "if the occupant of the center doesn't or, even more, can't, name his successor, that derogates from his authority, because everyone obeying him now is simultaneously scrambling around trying to find whom they might be able to recognize as a successor." ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-3))

In a 40-person company, a fight between your two most senior people over a new product line is very likely also a fight over who stands next to you. The product is where the unspoken succession question has surfaced. So the decision you make is also a ranking, and you should make it as one, openly.

## Monday

What follows is my application of these concepts to a firm your size. Katz writes at the level of states and institutions, not management practice, so read it as a translation into your setting.

**1. Hear each of them separately, as a judge.** Turn each person's demand into a question. Ask each to describe the product succeeding a year from now, what its lead would need from you to get there, and who on the team they would develop to take over from them. That last question tests the thing Katz cares most about. Succession in perpetuity means choosing "not just... the best person for this job right now, but the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). A candidate who can only describe themselves at the center is showing you something important.

**2. Decide, and give the winner real power.** "It is immoral to give someone responsibility for doing something without giving them the power to do it" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-61)). Name one lead and state, in specific terms, what they control: hiring for the product, the roadmap, and the budget line. Do not give them the title while keeping the decisions yourself.

**3. Rank the other person openly and give them a real post.** This is the part people usually skip. Katz's model is that "Each institution has a head, and this head has an appointed successor," and that "the appointed successor will be assessed and replaced regularly" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). Say plainly that the second person is next in line for this product, or for something larger, and give them a defined area of command that is theirs and not a role as deputy-in-waiting. Make clear that the ranking can be revised. "The selection would not be made once and for all" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-8)). Revisability should not be read as instability: "it can be a sign of deep reserves of trust and experienced cooperation" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-5)).

**4. Make it a public event.** Announce it to the company yourself, framed in terms of continuity: what the product is for, who leads it, and who follows. A back-room decision lets the result look like a private victory. A public naming makes it your act, which is exactly what you want people to see.

**5. Give the person who lost a better path than resentment.** Katz's phrase is "donate your resentment to the center." Concretely, that means obeying so well that you put yourself in a strong position for later: "this approach of hyper-obedience even positions you better for the replacement of the occupant of the center by a substantially better one, who could presumably see what you were doing" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-16)). You can tell them, in your own words, that the best way to lead next time is to make the current lead succeed and to let you see it. If they leave instead, that tells you something about whether they could have held the center.

**6. Watch your own reaction.** Katz writes that "The center doesn't resent—that would serve as a definition of the center. But, of course, any occupant of the center will resent" ([Tokenization](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)). You will probably feel irritated with both of them. Keep it out of the judgment. As the person deciding, you can't afford to take a side out of pique.

## Read next

- [The Pointman](/post/the-pointman): how Katz arrives at the term, and why it involves both taking the initiative and becoming a target.
- [Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession): the fullest picture of ranked, revisable successors and "controlled usurpation" between teams, which fits a small company better than you might expect.

A question for you before Monday: if you were hit by a bus on Tuesday, whom would you want running the company, and do either of these two know your answer? If they don't, that uncertainty may be what they are really fighting about.

rows.q: Explain how the ostensive, imperative and declarative relate to Katz's account of money as debt to the center, for someone who knows Girard well but has never read Gans.
rows.a:
## Starting from what you know: where Gans parts from Girard

For a Girardian the quickest way in is the point where Gans corrects Girard. Katz states it bluntly: "there’s no reason why some animal group, even an exceptionally intelligent one, should view ganging up on and killing one of its members as “meaningful,” which is to say, “memorable.”" Gans first added a sign to the end of the lynching, and then saw that "if the real point is the pointing, the killing itself is superfluous" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38)).

So the originary scene keeps Girard's mimetic crisis but changes how it ends. The group converges on a desired object, usually food, and the convergence overrides the animal pecking order. One member hesitates, the others imitate the hesitation, and "This, what Gans calls “the gesture of aborted appropriation,” is the first sign" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-5)). The object that held them back becomes the center, the first sacred thing. Then the group eats it together.

You can already see debt in this. Katz: "in deferral we remain indebted, to each other and to the center through each other: the shared object is a gift from the center and sharing it is how we pay or, rather, pay down, the debt." He goes so far as to say "debt is the tokenization of deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). Girard's founding debt is guilt for a murder that has been covered up. Katz's founding debt is gratitude, and an obligation, toward the thing that let you eat without killing each other.

## The three speech forms

Gans's other contribution, in *The Origin of Language*, is an account of how the higher forms of speech grow out of that first sign. Katz treats this sequence as a grammar of every social relation. The rule throughout is that no one sets out to invent the next form. A mistake threatens the scene, and someone repairs it in a way that turns out to be new.

**Ostensive.** This is the pointing-and-naming sign, the first one. It is not neutral description. Naming something protects it: "An object pointed to, referred to, named, is thereby protected, at the very least insofar as we are enjoined to observe rather than appropriate it" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-9)). A command is already folded into the ostensive.

**Imperative.** This form begins with an "inappropriate ostensive": "One member of the community issues the ostensive sign in the absence of the object, and another member of the community then supplies the object" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-1)). Nobody meant to give a command, but a command now exists. Once humans can command, they command the center and the center commands them. Katz calls the result *imperative exchange*: "if we do what God says we can expect our requests to Him to be honored" ([Felicity](/post/felicity#p-11)).

This is the point where grammar becomes economy. Ritual is imperative exchange: you give the center what it prescribes and you ask for continued provision. "The center distributes… This is a gift economy, or what I have been calling imperative exchange" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-6)). Debt in its first form is a set of commands and petitions running both ways between the community and its center.

This is also where Katz places Girard's sacrificial violence, not at the beginning but as a later escalation of debt. Following Gans, he holds that the earliest humans had animal deities, "with human sacrifice coming at a much later, imperial state." His explanation is in terms of debt: "As we get more and more distant from the center, and the interval between debt issuance and dischargement grows, the debt become overwhelming, even unbearable, to the point where even the sacrifice of the first-born to the God-emperor is not enough" ([Data as Currency and the Debt to the Center](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)). Read this way, the scapegoat is what happens when a debt to the center grows too large to pay.

**Declarative.** The declarative grows out of an imperative that cannot be fulfilled because the object isn't there. The demand stretches into a question. The reply repeats the object's name together with a "don't." Katz adds his own twist to Gans here: the "don't" points two ways. "Insofar as “don’t” is directed towards the imperator/interrogator, it is issuing a counter imperative to cease demanding the object. Insofar as it is directed toward the object, it is commanding the object to absent itself from the scene" ([A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-21)). The only one who can order an object away is the center, so the first statement of fact says, in effect, "stop demanding, because *reality* has dictated otherwise" ([p-23](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social#p-23)).

## Declarative as credit, money as declarative

Put these together and the link to money follows. A declarative defers a demand by appealing to an order behind the scene that holds for everyone. That is also what credit does. "Credit is the creation of terms under which immediate demands can be deferred" ([Style](/post/style-markers-and-measurements-of-deferral#p-5)). Katz states it outright: "to speak in sentences is to draw upon and issue lines of credit. The debt we owe to the center is a product of deferral, and the lines of credit issued are therefore tokenized deferrals" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-8)).

Money is this structure made into a physical object. Katz adopts Gans's definition from Gans's essay "On Firstness," saying it would be hard to improve on: money "is a credit drawn on the sacred that cannot be freely reproduced" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-8)). He then takes it further than Gans. Gans thought market exchange cut loose from the originary scene because the debt is paid "at once." Katz and Baker argue that the instantaneous coffee purchase is the exception. Loans, wages, pensions, insurance and the lender of last resort all live in the *interval* between a debt and its payment. Money, then, is not a measure of value; it is "metonymy, a means to sequence debt denomination and discharge" ([p-30](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-30)). From Christine Desan's history they take the origin of money as a receipt issued by the center: "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center, and that record can in turn become a way of paying debts to the center" ([p-36](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)).

You can map the three forms onto a single banknote:

- **Ostensive:** it is a token that points to the center that issued it. That is why counterfeiting is a profanation and not just theft.
- **Imperative:** it carries the center's command (pay your taxes in this) and your petition back (honor it when I spend it). Katz notes that "An imperative… always looks forward to some exchange" ([Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-6)).
- **Declarative:** it promises that the order which issued it will still exist when you spend it. It is "a system of promises backed by sovereignty" ([p-38](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-38)), and for that reason "credit… is always a bet on succession" ([Perfecting the Imperative](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-9)). Hyperinflation is the declarative failing: reality no longer backs the deferral.

The last connection for a Girardian is that Katz finds the scapegoat inside modern finance as well. The state becomes "primarily a debt enforcement agency." Politics comes down to which part of the population will bear enforcement, and the money order runs on "rituals of desecration" in which "everyone can hope all their debts will be imposed on the other party" ([p-51](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-51)). This is mimetic rivalry over who carries the debt.

## Where to go next

- **[There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf)**, Katz's essay written with Zack Baker. It is the full argument, moving through Gans, Desan, Drumm's "outside spread" and derivatives as ritual.
- **[A Grammar of the Social](/post/anthropomorphics-a-grammar-of-the-social)**, from *Anthropomorphics*. It gives the most careful derivation of the three speech forms and Katz's reading of the two-way "don't."

A question to take with you: Girard reads the Passion as the exposure of the scapegoat. Katz says the Axial Age turns imperative exchange into "complete devotion" offered with no expectation of return ([Perfecting the Imperative](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-19)). In that light, is a debt that can never be repaid a revelation or a trap, and what would a currency built on it look like?

rows.q: Trace how the concept of the center changes from Anthropomorphics to the recent essays on thirdness and data exchange. What stayed, and what was dropped?
rows.a:
## The short version

Across the whole span, the center stays the condition of everything human: it is where agency, imperatives, distribution and debt come from, and succession is the test of whether it holds. What changes is where Katz locates it and how it works. In *Anthropomorphics* the center is mainly a figure, a sovereign or occupant who issues imperatives. In the recent essays it becomes increasingly a process: an intelligence assembled from data, reached through the juridical, and paid in samples rather than money. Some positions were dropped outright, and others survive only in reworked form.

## What stayed

**The center comes before the human.** In *Anthropomorphics*: "It is the center, first of all, that has agency—human agency will later come to be modeled on the agency of the center" ([The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-19)). Looking back in 2025, Katz says the book's title was meant to stress exactly this: "we were always already imitating the center that was itself nothing more than a vectorization of our converging desires turned back at us through a prohibition" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)).

**The center speaks, and we relay it.** The book ends on this: "All we can say (through whatever media) is what the center has us say, and that the center has us say it" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-21)). The 2024 essays say the same thing in new terms: "Thinking always comes from the center, and the center, as the depository of converged and abstracted discourses mediated by various chains of command, is always ahead of us" ([Muffled Transmission](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-1)). In 2025 Katz pushes it further, to "“us” being nothing more than the center speaking to itself," and admits he had long held back from that formulation because it "sounded to me too mystical or Hegelian" ([Measuring Deferral](/post/measuring-deferral#p-13)).

**The center distributes, so we are in its debt.** In *Anthropomorphics*, "The center distributes" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-6)). The later work turns this into a full theory of debt: "we’re all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)).

**Succession is the test.** "The solution I propose: the current occupant of the center chooses his successor" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-2)). This becomes "singularized succession in perpetuity" and stays the guiding thread of everything after.

## What changed

**1. From "occupant" to pointman, dictator, and central intelligence.** The book's main tool is the split between the *signifying* center (meaning, sacral origin) and the *occupied* center (whoever actually rules): "One’s place in relation to the signifying center is fundamentally questionable, even if one’s relation to the occupied center is not—hence the discrepancy" ([Talk of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-talk-of-the-center#p-1)). The later essays rename the occupant: "I can now replace the clumsy “occupant of the center” with “pointman”" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)), and elsewhere "dictator" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1)). More importantly, the occupant stops being simply a person. "Central intelligence does and should govern, with the director of central intelligence the pointman" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-11)). The center itself is now "the result of continual sifting, filtering, testing, mapping, simulating performed on data," and "the center is whatever will turn out to have been furthest upstream of that" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3), [p-5](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-5)). By 2026, sovereignty itself becomes data-security firms "returning them to what sovereignty has always been—the largest property owner, establishing and presiding over the nomos" ([Deferral and Appropriation](/post/deferral-and-appropriation-property-and-the-center#p-15)).

**2. The two-centers problem is recast.** The signifying/occupied pair is not abandoned, but a second division sits beside it: "the center as generative origin continued through the occupied social center, on the one hand, and the center as anything upon which joint attention is exercised" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-3)). In another essay he describes this as the originary object being "both the thing we attend to and the meta-person we obey and participate in," two features that "get separated" over history ([The Sample as Our Donation to the Center](/post/the-sample-as-our-donation-to-the-center#p-6)). In this framing, our service to the center runs through the smaller centers: "we serve the center and donate our resentments to it through the curation of those samples as data" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-3)).

**3. The juridical moves to the middle.** In *Anthropomorphics*, the human sciences study "the difference between the imperatives issued by central authority and the imperatives obeyed by lower authorities" ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-4)). The book has courts, but they sit at the edge of its account. The Thirdness essays put them at the heart: "we place the juridical at the center—the juridical is the form taken for the settling of resentments" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-7)). Judgment is then to be converted into "each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)).

**4. Money moves from delegation to something to abolish.** In 2019, "Money is a means of subordinating market activity to central authority—that is, money is a form taken by the delegation of power" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-17)). Later, "the thinking of singularized succession, then, must involve thinking the abolition of money" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-2)). Rankings of possible successors take over the job prices do: "These constant fluctuations in succession replicate price change" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)).

## What was dropped

Read the next points as my reading of the shift, not as Katz's own retractions. In several places he reworks a position rather than repudiating it.

**The ban on accusing the center.** The book is categorical: "What is absolutely forbidden under such an order is directing violent centralization toward the authorities" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-13)). The later Katz builds a legal channel for exactly that pressure: "in place of the sacrifice of the central figure we have the high stakes lawsuit against him" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)). The accuser takes on matching risk, through the possibility that the president could "impose further penalties on those participating in a failed impeachment" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-17)). The position has reversed, but the purpose has not: the lawsuit is meant to defer the scapegoating of the center, not to license it.

**Candidates kept away from power.** In the book, the way to stop rivalry among successors was "to prohibit the top-tier candidates from occupying positions in which they exercise any real power" ([Maintaining the Present](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-9)). The later model expects frequent hand-offs and even "introducing a bit of randomness into the selection process" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-13)). A stable, slow succession has become one that moves all the time and works like a market.

**The sacral leftover.** *Anthropomorphics* already says it is not restoring the sacred, but it still thinks in terms of signifying versus occupied center, a split inherited from sacral kingship. The 2026 essay begins: "Center Study has no political theology" ([Deferral and Appropriation](/post/deferral-and-appropriation-property-and-the-center#p-1)). The sacral vocabulary gives way to debt, credit and data.

**One clarification that refines rather than drops.** "The center doesn’t resent—that would serve as a definition of the center. But, of course, any occupant of the center will resent" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)). This keeps the old distinction between the center and its occupant, but states it more sharply than the book did.

## What to read next

- [Learncoin](/post/learncoin) states the "two centers" problem most directly and shows the center paid in samples instead of money.
- [Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession) shows the pointman, central intelligence and successor-rankings fitting together as one replacement for the market.

**An exercise.** Take one passage from [Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center) and rewrite it in the vocabulary of the 2025 succession essays: pointman, ranked successors, lawsuit, data. Then note what the old version can say that the new one can't. That remainder is a good measure of what was lost in the shift.

rows.q: What exactly is idiomclining, how is it different from coining jargon, and can you idiomcline this sentence of mine: "Our team needs better communication"?
rows.a:
## What idiomclining is

The word combines "idiom" and "cline." A cline is a gradual slope along which language shifts without anyone quite noticing. Linguists use it for *grammaticization*, the process by which a full word wears down into a grammatical function. "Going to" (travel) became "gonna" (future tense).

In an earlier essay Katz proposed running that slope backwards, which he called "upclining." In an upcline, "a word is deliberately removed from a circulation that splinters its uses, and placed within a new circulation, or idiom, that treats the word as a prompt for a new hierarchy of declaratives, imperatives and ostensives" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-49)). This is "a retrieval forward, not a recovery of the identical meaning" ([p-43](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-43)).

The 2026 essay generalizes the idea. Idiomclining means "setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17)). Katz chose "upcline" as a way of resisting "the more passive 'incline' and catastrophic 'decline'" ([p-16](/post/idiomclining#p-16)).

Why bother? Katz starts from Goodhart's Law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops working as a measure. He argues "every single word, expression or sentence is or contains measures that are liable to become targets" ([p-1](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). Words like "critical thinking" become checklists that people perform. Idiomclining is the countermove, and Katz offers it explicitly as a replacement: "'idiomclining' instead of 'critical thinking' or other bureaucratized categories designed for mass test taking" ([p-17](/post/idiomclining#p-17)).

Two features matter for your exercise:

- **It is always a bit mistaken, and that is the point.** You violate a convention, "but you also can't go wrong because you present a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others" ([p-17](/post/idiomclining#p-17)). An idiomcline is an offer made on a scene, and it is tested by what others do with it.
- **It pulls in two directions at once.** You want to make your idiom "both more idiomatic and more transferable" ([p-15](/post/idiomclining#p-15)). It should be precise to this conversation and this occasion, yet portable enough for the other person to carry it elsewhere.

## How it differs from coining jargon

Katz is not simply anti-jargon. He grants that "what seems like unintelligible jargon is very often a way of phrasing some claim that has resulted from the cumulative responses to attacks on a dozen previous ways of phrasing it" ([The Meaning of Meaning](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-4)). He defends his own specialized vocabulary as *compression*, a store of shared reference points ([Compression](/post/compression#p-9)).

The trouble starts when the coinage freezes. Three differences follow from that.

**Function.** Katz quotes Alice Becker-Ho on what jargon does. "The basic aim of these jargons is to come across as a specialist." Jargon "defends and reinforces a world based on the division of labor by protecting the privileges of a caste" ([Becker-Ho review](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review#p-10)). Jargon marks distance. Idiomclining aims to be picked up and carried.

**Direction of the imperative.** Katz warns that "nominalization can freeze discourse into jargon." Breaking jargon up is "a question of refusing the imperatives the nominalizations start giving you" ([Technology and Magic](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings#p-21)). An imperative exchange here means a tacit deal: do X, expect Y in return. A frozen term lures you into the belief that renaming the problem solves it. Idiomclining turns nouns back into verbs, scenes and commands.

**Idioms can harden too.** Center Study's own vocabulary can "become so formulaic as to mark belonging to a impenetrable bureaucratic space. There must always be space for idiom generation within the idiom" ([Idiomclining, p-10](/post/idiomclining#p-10)). This matters for your sentence, because the easiest mistake is to swap your words for Katz's.

## Working your sentence: "Our team needs better communication"

**1. Spot the frozen piece.** "Communication" is on Katz's list. He names his "hostility to words like 'cognition,' 'consciousness,' 'belief,' 'communication'" ([p-1](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). It is a measure that has become a target. You can hold more meetings, send more messages and run more check-ins, and "communication" improves on paper while nothing changes.

"Better" is a comparison with no stated standard. "Needs" is a demand addressed to no one in particular. Katz suggests a discipline here: "obey the constraint to not say that distant, abstract others 'should…'" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-18)).

**2. First, the jargon version, as a warning.** "Our team has an unresolved imperative gap in its ostensive-imperative circuits." This uses real Center Study terms and adds nothing. It swaps one target for another and makes the speaker look like a specialist. That is exactly the move to avoid.

**3. Find the scene.** Ask what happened that made you say this. Katz's standard question is "who would have to be making which decisions, and with what effectivity, so as produce what you would see as the event you are hoping for" ([Muffled Transmission](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-4)).

"Communication" usually covers two things:

- **An imperative gap.** This is the distance between what someone was asked to do and what they did.
- **An unnamed center.** A team, Katz says, needs to be "very clear about qualifications and roles" ([Hostages, Proxies, and Moles](/post/hostages-proxies-and-moles#p-5)). "Communication" is often a polite way of not saying who decides.

**4. Retrieve the word forward.** "Communicate" comes from the Latin *communicare*, "to make common." That etymology is general knowledge, not from the archive, though Katz makes the same kind of move with "sample" ([The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-18)).

What a team needs in common is not talk but objects everyone can point to and call *the same*. Katz's model is the surgeon's "Scalpel… Scalpel," from which he concludes that "every met imperative includes an at least tacit confirmation" ([Perfecting the Imperative](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-2)). You ask for the thing, it is handed over, and both of you name it as the same.

**5. Some idiomclined candidates.** Each is in the present tense, as Katz recommends ([Compression](/post/compression#p-11)):

- *"We say different things about the same task, so we do it twice or not at all."* This bends Katz's formula, "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)), back onto your case.
- *"Every request here ends when the asker points at the finished thing and says: that's it."* Here the confirming ostensive becomes a team practice.
- *"Whoever asks, show what done looks like; whoever is asked, say it back."* This adapts Katz's line: "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)).

Your demand for "better communication" turns out to be a demand for a clearer *command*. Katz puts it this way: "whatever your demand of the center, consider the kind of command that could limit and satisfy it better than it would itself know how to and then realize that your demand is really for such a command" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-17)).

Notice that none of these candidates needs the vocabulary of Center Study to be understood. That is what keeps them transferable. Each is also probably wrong in some detail. The test is to say one to your team and watch the adjusted response.

## Read next

- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) in full. It is short. Paragraphs 11 to 14, on the dangerous scene versus the buffered scene, show that idiomclining is also about reading how much is at stake in a situation.
- [Attentionality and Originary Ethics: Upclining](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics), the essay that first develops the cline idea. Its account of distraction and fixation will sharpen your diagnosis of team "communication" failures.

**Exercise:** recall one concrete incident behind your sentence. Write down three things: the request as it was issued, what was actually done, and the moment someone could have said "this is the same" but didn't. Then write one present-tense sentence that names that moment. Make it one your team could repeat without you there.

rows.q: Is singularized succession in perpetuity just monarchism? Give the strongest version of that objection and then Katz's reply.
rows.a:
## Is singularized succession in perpetuity just monarchism?

First, the term itself. Singularized succession in perpetuity (Katz sometimes shortens it to "SSIP") is the idea that whoever occupies the center at any level names a single successor. That successor is chosen for being best able to choose the next successor, and so on indefinitely. Katz's starting point is a test of whether power is real: "the most certain test that power was in fact held was that the sovereign selected his successor. Otherwise, would it not be those who selected the successor who wielded power?" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)).

### The objection at full strength

**1. Its lineage is admittedly monarchical.** Katz says the concept came from "trying to think through the furthest implications of the absolutist politics" of *Anthropomorphics* ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). He writes that "monarchy is the only real form of governance—everything else is either mimicking monarchy or predicated on the endless struggle to prevent others from installing 'their' king" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-1)). He also adopts "dictator" as the plain name for whoever occupies the center ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1)).

**2. Replacing heredity with appointment is an old monarchical variant, not a new idea.** This point is mine, not the archive's. Adoptive succession has been tried many times: the Roman "five good emperors," papal and Ottoman arrangements, founder-designated heirs. The Roman sequence ended when Marcus Aurelius chose his son Commodus. Calling it "selection" leaves the essential structure unchanged: one will, accountable to nobody below it, decides the future.

**3. The checks are decorative.** Katz does allow the pointman to be sued. But he also gives the pointman the power to countersue, and he says that if a president could penalize those behind a failed removal attempt, "impeachment would become an entirely different proposition" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-17)). That design would deter challenges. The final word still belongs to the sovereign.

**4. Calling it "descriptive" shields it from criticism.** If everyone with any authority is "always already" trying to secure their succession, the concept can't be refuted. It can only be applied. A normative program is being passed off as a description.

**5. Spreading it to every institution multiplies the monarchy.** When every office, firm and school names its successor, you have kingship at every scale. Katz's own general claim about originary thinking was that it is "not intrinsically committed or opposed to monarchy or democracy" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-6)). It is hard to square that with his later claim that "there is nothing more to governance than singularized succession in perpetuity" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-1)).

### Katz's reply, assembled from the texts

**He accepts the lineage but rejects the regime type.** For him monarchy "remains a placeholder concept," useful in arguments with democrats. But "we're in uncharted waters here and must be prepared to think in terms of a continuum of possibilities of rule." That continuum runs from primogeniture at one end to fast handoffs between specialists at the other, like a manager bringing in relief pitchers ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4)). What sets SSIP apart is that "the multiplication of succession rituals would distinguish this order from monarchy, which has few and regularly set succession rituals (coronations)" ([#p-3](/post/continuum-of-power#p-3)). Monarchism usually draws its appeal from sacral kingship, and Katz rules that out: "retaining sacral kingship, much less restoring it, cannot be considered an option" ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-2)). In his model, occupation of the center is "completely desacralized and de-divinized... and reduced to functionality" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-5)).

**Heredity is the thing he is moving away from.** The concept "cuts against, without excluding... primogeniture, since succession is now understood as the outcome of competition and mentorship" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). Hereditary monarchy does solve the succession problem, "but in such a way as to generate other problems." Katz also says it is "a mistake to invest one's thought in a single, rigidly defined form of order" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). The designation can be revised at any time. In the later essays the published, changing rankings of successors are meant to work like a price system, a "digital bulletin board (on which we would see fluctuations, like stock prices, which these nominations would replace)" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-6)). Read this way, SSIP is as much a theory of value and credit set against capital's discounting of the future as a regime proposal.

**"In perpetuity" carries the weight.** The question is not who rules now. "it's not just a question of choosing the best person for this job right now, but the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). That is why he calls it "the umbilical cord linking us to the originary scene" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-2)). The originary imperative is to keep the scene, and so the deferral, going. Succession is that same imperative extended through time.

**Being descriptive is the point.** He holds the concept "both normative and diagnostic: a flawed society is one in which succession is not attended to and accounted for and a pathological society is one in which succession is actually subverted" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-13)). It is meant as a lens for any institution. He even says liberal and left institutions "understand succession far better than the right side of liberalism" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)).

**It applies to practices, not only to thrones.** "You could define a practice in terms of the singularization of the one who will succeed it" ([Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics#p-27)). At the level of the individual it shades into "selving," the work of staying the same over time: explicit naming of a successor is still recommended, "but it should also make it unnecessary" ([Selving](/post/selving#p-22)). A monarchist wants a king. SSIP asks a teacher or a founder who will carry the work on, and whether that person could find the next one.

**The sacrifice is replaced, not removed.** In the succession ritual, "in place of the sacrifice of the central figure we have the high stakes lawsuit against him, which might be brought by any subject," and a successful challenger is the obvious heir ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)). Once losing power no longer means dying, "power can be passed around with facility," which brings the model close to sortition, selection by lot ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-12)).

**It is formal about content.** SSIP rules out no ethnic, religious or experimental basis for an order. It asks you to find "the most unbroken chain of transmissions of power from the origin of the social until now" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-10)).

### Where the objection still has force

On points 1, 2 and 4, Katz's reply works. SSIP is less a regime than a criterion for judging any institution, and it is deliberately desacralized. Points 3 and 5 hold up better. His answer to "what about bad rulers?" rests on two assumptions. One is that only someone who really holds power could make a designation stick. The other is that elites would rally around the office even under a malevolent occupant ([Sufficiency, p-7 and p-12](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-7)). Those are empirical bets. And he calls the concept "the most anti or non-liberal concept possible" ([SSIP](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)), which is a long way from the neutrality he claimed for originary thinking in 2021. A fair summary: it is not monarchism, but it is unapologetically centered on the singular power that monarchy historically represented.

**Read next:** [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity) gives his fullest defense, including the "bad leader" problem. [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power) explains why "monarchy" is only a placeholder.

**Exercise:** pick an institution you know well. Who is its successor, actually or in practice? Then ask whether that person could themselves choose well. In Katz's terms, the answer tells you whether the institution is flawed, pathological or sound.

rows.q: Take the essays on Judaism as a civilizational blockchain. What is the argument, and how does it follow from the originary hypothesis?
rows.a:
## The argument

"Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain" (2025) begins with antisemitism and ends with a proposal for what Jews should take themselves to be for. The central move is to describe hatred of Jews as a logic, not as a feeling or a prejudice.

**1. The Jew as scandal.** Katz drops "antisemitism," which slides toward "racism" and toward official definitions, and describes a structure instead: "The existence of Jews is a scandal, and therefore their existence is an unmistakable sign of immeasurable and monstrous Jewish power" ([Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-1)). The structure is circular and points outside the law. If Jews control the system, justice cannot be had inside it, so "to get at the Jew systemic norms and guardrails must be disregarded, even torn down" ([p-2](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-2)). Jew-hatred is a demand to leave the juridical order and return to the vendetta.

**2. The fantasy collapses once you try to act on it.** "If the Jews really control everything, there's nothing you can do; if you can do something, they don't really control everything but, rather, represent one of many power centers" ([p-3](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-3)). Once power is something you could measure, against the Qataris, the Five Eyes, the hundreds of other lobbies ([p-16](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-16)), the totalizing claim has to give way. So it can produce low-level violence and hostility, but it cannot reach the level where states are actually decided.

**3. From the enemy's logic to a Jewish vocation.** This is the turn. If the war on Jews is a comprehensive vendetta, then it "does suggest a kind of vocation for the Jews themselves: maintaining all the institutional means of deferring vendetta" ([p-6](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-6)). Katz adds that Jews cannot simply ask to be left alone: "the Jews have no choice but to represent something" ([p-8](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-8)). If they will be a sign either way, they should choose which sign.

**4. Witnessing, narrowed.** He takes up the old idea that being Jewish means bearing witness to injustice, but he cuts off the leftist reading of it as "social justice." He limits it "strictly to the operation of the juridical within the terms of the nomos, which is to say perversions and travesties of justice within the strict sense of a court case with opposing sides" ([p-9](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-9)). The nomos is the originary distribution of land and authority that every later dispute refers back to.

**5. The blockchain.** Hence the image: "Jews should try to become a civilizational blockchain—recording social exchanges and disputes as objectively and permanently as we can" ([p-11](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-11)). The image works because "the blockchain is where covenants can be recorded in a permanent, inalterable manner" ([p-12](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-12)), and the covenant is the thing Judaism has kept. Katz therefore prefers "a nation of scribes" to "a nation of priests" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)). He offers this as a rule for relations with Gentiles: "we will mark your treatment of us on the scale of justice while marking as deviant anyone claiming adherence to Judaism who seeks to undermine covenants, or contracts or agreements" ([p-14](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-14)).

**6. What exactly gets recorded.** The ledger is not mainly a list of grievances. It records the shadow that the alternative logic casts over the law, the logic of hostage-taking, "you must hunt the Jews or be hunted yourself as a Jew." What must be recorded is the "ever present 'penumbra' of another possibility against the terms of juridical order" ([p-19](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-19)).

## How it follows from the originary hypothesis

The blockchain essay does not set out this derivation itself; it takes it for granted. You can reconstruct it from the essays around it. Here is the chain as I read it across those texts.

**Representation is the deferral of violence, and the scene must stay "the same."** On the originary scene the sign holds off the convergence on the center. Every later institution keeps that deferral going and has to show that it continues the one before. Katz defines meaning this way: to mean something is to "'insist' that what you have uttered will be insisted to be the 'same' by other language users in situations that will likewise be determinable to be the 'same'" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-11)). A blockchain is a technology for exactly that kind of verified sameness over time.

**The juridical is a scaled-up form of deferral.** Once the Big Man occupies the center and empires form, the vendetta has to be capped. Katz defines the juridical "as placing a ceiling on the vendetta by introducing higher order arbitration at those points where the vendetta threatens to undo imperial order; while, on the other end, preserving what is ultimately a ritually enacted originary nomos" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-1)). So when he says the Jewish vocation is to maintain "the institutional means of deferring vendetta," he is placing Jews at the point where originary deferral takes its post-tribal, imperial form.

**Violent centralization always looks for a hidden center.** In *Anthropomorphics*, the most dangerous target of violent centralization is the center itself. These convergences "always, at whatever scale, seek to find and punish a hidden power imagined to lie behind the scenes of the official power" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-13)). Jew-hatred is a pure case of this. Elsewhere Katz says "'antisemitism' is really about giving a name to hidden sources of power, which in the West always involves some kind of 'prosecution' of 'tyrants'" ([The Political Infrastructure of Judaism](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-3)). He also says it "exploits real or perceived gaps between the purported powers delegated to or claimed by social institutions and the actions carried out by those institutions" ([Antisemitism and Power](/post/antisemitism-and-power#p-2)). The scapegoat logic from the originary scene, now aimed at an imagined usurper, is what the ledger exists to record.

**Judaism as a title deed, and therefore as ledgering.** Following Bernard Lamborelle, Katz reads the Abrahamic covenant as originally a land grant from an earthly emperor. Over many exiles it was raised into a covenant with God, the King of Kings, while the attachment to a particular land remained ([The Longest, Most Convoluted… Title Deed](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack#p-1)). On this reading the Hebrew Bible is a continual effort at "'proving' that those of us in possession of these documents… are, in fact, the 'same' people" ([p-11](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack#p-11)). That is the originary problem of sameness over time, worked out as an inheritance. Since "the first writing is the first designation of property and the first token of exchange and issuance of debt" ([Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-1)), scribes are ledger-keepers of the debt to the center. In "A Cybernetics of Judaism" he says it directly: "A nation of priests became a nation of scribes which means a nation of ledgerers" ([A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-6)).

**Chosenness redefined as responsibility for deferral.** The same essay translates the theology: "God's voice is whatever tells us when and how to defer violence, or when and how we are failing to do so. … Jews are more than anyone else responsible for deferring violence—therein are we 'chosen'" ([A Cybernetics of Judaism, p-9](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-9)). The vendettas against Jews also "tend to be leading indicators" of mob formation more generally ([p-17](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-17)). This is why Jewish record-keeping matters beyond Jews.

Put together: the originary scene gives deferral and the center. The empire gives the juridical as the institution that caps the vendetta. Judaism, as a covenant kept through scribes, specializes in the record that shows the order is still "the same." Jew-hatred is the vendetta aimed at an imagined hidden center. The vocation follows from this: keep the record that makes the juridical order hold, and record the shadow of the vendetta against it. Katz's most compressed version is that Jews "serve as a meter measuring this gap," the gap between power and legitimacy ([The Political Infrastructure of Judaism, p-27](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-27)).

## Where to push back

"Follows" may be too strong. The originary hypothesis supplies the frame: deferral, center, juridical, ledger. The specific claims rest on further premises Katz brings in from elsewhere: the Lamborelle reading, the "normative Jew" as "the observant Zionist living in Israel" ([p-7](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-7)), and proposals such as excluding pro-Palestinian Jews from Judaism ([p-10](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-10)). Katz presents these as contributions from "no Jewish 'leader'" and admits he is not deducing them. He also notes the tension at the heart of the role: a blockchain "involves exercising power, and exercising power involves being involved in power struggles" ([p-15](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-15)). That tension, between the neutral recorder and the interested party, is the place to probe.

## What to read next

- [A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism): the fuller statement of Jews as a "governance technology," of persecution as chastisement for failures of deferral, and of rethinking the Messiah as whoever leaves an intact chain of succession.
- [The Longest, Most Convoluted, Revised and Thickly Imagined Title Deed Possible](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack): the reading of the Hebrew Bible that the blockchain image rests on.

As an exercise, take a current accusation against Israel or Jews that you have seen and ask what entry a "civilizational blockchain" would make for it. It is not enough to say whether the accusation is true or false. Ask where it falls between a dispute that could be settled in court and a demand that takes the court out of the picture.

rows.q: On Katz's account, why can a language model write fluent declaratives but not promise or deem? Does that argument hold up?
rows.a:
## Katz's argument

Katz's case does not depend on what the machine feels. It depends on where a speech act sits in the grammar of the center, and on who can be held to it.

**Why the declarative comes easily.** For Center Study the declarative is the speech form that can be lifted out of its scene. Under orality it stayed close to oaths, curses and prayers, and "the declarative would become isolatable and analyzable as a speech form in the wake of writing" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-2)). Literacy then turned that detachability into an ideal: "the ideal declarative sentence is one that could be uttered felicitously by anyone, anywhere, at any time" ([An Introduction to Disciplinarity](/post/introduction-to-disciplinarity#p-87)). A language model trained on the written archive is close to a literal "anyone, anywhere." It has absorbed what Katz, following David Olson, calls the metalanguage of literacy, the "assumes," "suggests," "implies" apparatus that makes a sentence look as if it needs no speaker. In that sense the model is metaphysics put on a machine. Katz takes Gans's definition of metaphysics as "the assumption of the linguistic primacy of the declarative sentence," and adds that "the declarative cut off from the ostensive and imperative cannot acknowledge mimesis" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-5)). Fluency in that register is exactly what the training produces.

**Why promising and deeming are different.** These belong to what Katz calls the ostensive-imperative-ostensive sphere. In that sphere a pointing or naming issues a command, and the command is confirmed when someone points again. Speech in this sphere does something on a scene rather than describing one. In the Officer Class curriculum essay he groups them together: "promise, prayer, oath, curse, bless, oblige, thank, grace" ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-13)). Their force comes from indebtedness:

- **Promising.** "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)). So promising, indebting and issuing credit "cannot be reduced to computation, and are therefore the domain of decision." Prediction alone is not enough, because the predictability that institutions run on requires "humans to be reliable before they are predictable" (same essay, [p-12](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-12)).
- **Deeming.** "AIs can't 'deem,' or if they do deem, they have been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human" ([Toward a Curriculum](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12)). Deeming, he writes, "places us in the chain of originary debt to the center," and "there's really no particularly good reason why we should accept deeming carried out by a computer program or algorithm" ([p-13](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-13)).

Beneath both sits his deepest claim, from the essay on brute-force computation: "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation, which is the source of all human creation" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23)). A promise is a deferral you stake yourself on. You hold back now and put yourself in debt for later. The model has no appetite to defer and no share of the distribution it could lose. In his words it is not "'marked up' indelibly" as we are ([p-26](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-26)).

## Does it hold up?

My view is that it holds where it is a claim about standing, and wobbles where it is a claim about detection.

**The strong part.** Katz deliberately avoids the "it doesn't really feel it" move. He grants that an AI can join reflections and then asks, "what does our 'really feeling' amount to" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23)). So the argument is not about inner states. It is about whether a speech act opens a line of credit that can be enforced or forgiven. That is a juridical and scenic question, close to Austin's felicity conditions, which come up in the [Lecture 2](/post/mimetic#p-10) discussion of speech act theory. Asked that way, the answer is fairly plain. Nothing in the model can be held to the promise. When the chatbot "promises," the debt falls on the company that deployed it, which is Katz's point about authorization.

**The weak part.** He also says "there will always be something 'off' that humans can detect, even if not describe," and admits this is a hypothesis he has "no idea how to prove or disprove" ([Toward a Curriculum](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). His own work warns against exactly this kind of claim. Lists of human-only capacities "merely provide a menu of AI improvements for the next generation of programmers to attempt" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-10)). The urge to fix a human/machine boundary "merely inspires someone to try and automate that distinctively human feature" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-14)). By his own logic, a detectable "offness" is a temporary fact about current systems. He partly concedes this when he says these revisions of the Turing test "only really matter insofar as they provide models for performing our relations to the scenes we are on" ([p-15](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-15)). That moves the claim from description toward pedagogy.

**An open flank he raises himself.** The standing argument implies that the obstacle is institutional, not intrinsic. In the same essay on computation he discusses Agentic Protocols, "a self-developing AI driven entity that aims to have no human employees," with its own token and its own assets ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-13)). If such an entity can hold collateral, forfeit it and be sued, it can be placed in a chain of debt. Katz's reply at that point is normative: we have "no particularly good reason" to accept its deeming. That is a claim about which authority we should credit, not a claim that crediting is impossible. Note also that his line "being programmed negates those speech acts" ([p-17](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-17)) sits awkwardly with his radical view of mimesis, on which our own promises are iterations of everyone else's. The difference cannot be that humans are original. It has to be the stake.

**Where I think the argument actually leads.** Pushed consistently, it reaches further than Katz says, and that makes it stronger. On his account even a declarative is not just a well-formed string. Built into it is "the speaker implicitly leaving himself open to ostensive verification by virtue of the utterance" ([Political Syntax (III)](/post/political-syntax-iii-and-originary-thinking#p-6)). And the declarative is born from "an imperative that cannot be fulfilled" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-9)), that is, from a demand that was deferred. A model that never had a demand produces declarative form without declarative origin. So the clean contrast "fluent declaratives, but no promises" gives the model too much. It produces samples of all the speech forms, and the promise and the deeming are simply where the missing stake becomes impossible to hide. Katz's constructive answer fits this. The model's best use is as a medium for "the prolongation of intention" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-12)): it carries our promises and our predecessors' imperatives, while the debt stays with us.

## Where to go next

- [Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy), paragraphs 12–18: the deeming argument in full, and why he thinks it matters for training people rather than for settling what machines are.
- [Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah): promise as the originary speech act, blockchains as a way to "lock you in," and why reliability comes before predictability.

**An exercise:** take a promise made in an AI system's own voice, for example "I will remind you tomorrow." Trace who is actually indebted, who could enforce the promise or forgive it, and at what point a human deemed the system fit to speak that way. Then ask what would have to change in that chain for the promise to be the machine's own.
